title: Updating Documents
subtitle: updateOne, updateMany, upsert, and update operators
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Updating a database record often means changing just one or two fields — not replacing the entire document. Sending the whole document back wastes bandwidth and risks overwriting concurrent changes.
whyItExists.solution: MongoDB's update operators ($set, $inc, $push, $pull, etc.) perform surgical updates on specific fields. You describe what to change, not the full replacement document. This is atomic at the document level.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Use $set to update specific fields, $inc to increment counters, $push/$pull to modify arrays, $unset to remove fields. Use updateMany() for batch updates and upsert for create-or-update patterns.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If you need to completely replace a document (not just some fields), use replaceOne() instead of updateOne() with $set. Never update the _id field — it is immutable after insertion.

explainModes.beginner: Updating in MongoDB is like editing one cell in a spreadsheet without touching the rest of the row. You say 'change just the price to 899' and MongoDB changes only that field, leaving everything else untouched.
explainModes.simple: MongoDB update operators modify specific fields: $set changes a field's value, $inc increments a number, $push adds to an array, $pull removes from an array. updateOne() changes one document, updateMany() changes all matches.
explainModes.standard: MongoDB updates use an operator-based syntax where you describe the mutation, not the replacement. Operations are atomic at the document level — no partial updates. The upsert option inserts the document if no match is found.
explainModes.technical: MongoDB update operations are atomic at the single-document level. For multi-document atomicity, use transactions. The updateOne() and updateMany() methods accept a filter, an update document with operators, and options like upsert, arrayFilters, and hint. findOneAndUpdate() atomically updates and returns either the before or after document.
explainModes.deepDive: MongoDB's update operators are translated into internal mutation operations on the WiredTiger document. The oplog records each update as an idempotent operation using $set syntax, enabling replication. The $set operator creates a field if it doesn't exist. Update operators can be combined in a single update document — { $set: { field: v }, $inc: { counter: 1 } } — and they all execute atomically.

content.text: MongoDB provides four update methods: updateOne() modifies the first matching document, updateMany() modifies all matches, replaceOne() replaces the entire document (keeping the _id), and findOneAndUpdate() returns the document before or after updating it.
Use $addToSet instead of $push when you want array elements to remain unique. $push always appends, even if the value already exists.
An upsert (update + insert) inserts the document if no match is found, or updates it if a match exists. Set { upsert: true } as the third argument.

Using updateOne() without an operator (e.g., updateOne(filter, { name: 'Alice' })) will REPLACE the entire document, losing all other fields. Always use operators like $set inside the update document.

content.title: Practice Update Operators

questions.question: Which update operator increments a numeric field by a given amount?
questions.explanation: $inc increments (or decrements with a negative value) a numeric field. It's atomic, so it's safe for concurrent counters.

questions.question: What does the upsert option do in updateOne()?
options: Inserts the document if no match is found
Skips the update if the document already exists
questions.explanation: With { upsert: true }, MongoDB inserts a new document if the filter matches nothing, or updates the existing document if it finds a match.

questions.question: What is the difference between $push and $addToSet?
options: $push always appends; $addToSet only adds if the value isn't already in the array
$push adds to the front, $addToSet adds to the back
questions.explanation: $addToSet prevents duplicates — it only adds the element if it doesn't already exist in the array. $push always appends regardless.

faq.q: How do I update all documents in a collection?
faq.a: Use updateMany({}, { $set: { field: value } }) — the empty filter {} matches all documents. Be careful — this modifies every document in the collection.

faq.q: What is the difference between updateOne() and replaceOne()?
faq.a: updateOne() with operators ($set, $inc, etc.) modifies specific fields. replaceOne() replaces the ENTIRE document body (but preserves the _id). Use replaceOne() only when you intentionally want to swap out the whole document.

faq.q: How do I return the updated document after an update?
faq.a: Use findOneAndUpdate() with the option { returnDocument: 'after' }. This atomically updates the document and returns its new state. With returnDocument: 'before', you get the state before the update.

examples: E-commerce: { $inc: { stock: -1 } } when an order is placed
Task queue: findOneAndUpdate claims next pending task atomically without race conditions
